lesson.title: Updates close the door
lesson.subtitle: What an update fixes, and what to do when they stop

video.title: Updates close the door
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds; narration in the lesson language, captions as separate files.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher (main character)
Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Staff room, morning. Salma holds up her phone: a banner reads “Update ready”. Her thumb taps “Later”. A small counter above the phone shows 21 days.
scenes.animation: Banner slides down; thumb tap; counter ticks up.
scenes.narration: Every morning my phone says, “Update ready.” Every morning I press “Later”. It works fine, so why bother?

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the cyber track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: what an update really fixes, and what to do when the updates stop.

scenes.visual: A phone drawn as a house of code blocks. One block has a small gap. A maker hands over a patch block; a shadowy figure studies a copy of the patch, then looks around for houses still with the gap.
scenes.animation: Gap glows; patch slides in; figure's magnifying glass sweeps.
scenes.narration: Every app and every system has small mistakes in its code. Some of them are holes a criminal can use to get in. When the maker finds one, they send a fix: that’s a security update. But once the fix is out, attackers study it, and go looking for phones that haven’t installed it.

scenes.visual: The school store room door with a broken lock. Word spreads across the yard in speech bubbles. A new lock clicks into place.
scenes.animation: Speech bubbles hop from person to person; the new lock clicks.
scenes.narration: It’s like a broken lock on the school store room. Once everyone hears which lock is broken, that’s the first door a thief tries. An update is the new lock. Every day you wait, the door stays open.

scenes.visual: Clean card: a phone settings screen with two switches turning on, a moon, a charger and a Wi-Fi symbol, then a restart arrow.
scenes.animation: Switches flip on one by one; the restart arrow spins once.
scenes.narration: Turn on automatic updates, for the phone’s system and for your apps. Let them run at night, on the charger and on Wi-Fi, so they don’t eat your data. And when it asks to restart, say yes, because many fixes only start working after a restart.

scenes.visual: Salma in front of her class, glancing at her phone: “Update ready”, battery at 40%. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check. My phone says an update is ready, but I’m teaching all morning and my battery is at forty per cent. What should I do?

scenes.visual: The “tonight” card gets the check badge. A night sky over a phone on its charger, a Wi-Fi symbol beside it.
scenes.narration: Tonight, on the charger and on Wi-Fi. Not in the middle of a lesson, and not “never”. Most phones let you choose overnight updates, so you only decide once.

scenes.visual: A calendar page on a phone screen, labelled “Security update”. Older dates fade to grey; an old phone gets a small warning badge.
scenes.animation: Calendar pages flip back; the warning badge pops.
scenes.narration: Updates don’t last forever. One day, every phone and computer stops getting them. Look in Settings for the security update date, under About phone or Software update. If it’s more than a year old and no update is waiting, your phone has probably stopped getting fixes.

scenes.visual: The school office: an older desktop computer with a sticky note “Windows 10”. A calendar shows October 2025; paths branch from the computer: extended updates, an upgrade arrow, and a fence around email, banking and records.
scenes.animation: Paths draw out one by one.
scenes.narration: Many school computers still run Windows ten. It left normal support in October twenty twenty-five. Since then, it gets security updates only through Microsoft’s Extended Security Updates: home computers until October twenty twenty-seven, and organisations pay. Otherwise, move it to Windows eleven or another supported system. Until you can, keep it away from email, banking and pupils’ records.

scenes.visual: A shop counter labelled “Official store” on one side; on the other, a chat link, a box marked “modded” and a USB stick on a cyber café desk, each with a red cross.
scenes.animation: Red crosses stamp on one after another.
scenes.narration: Updates only protect what’s real. Get apps from the official store, never from a link in a chat. Say no to “modded” apps and cracked software: free copies of paid programs often hide malware. And be careful with USB sticks passed around at the cyber café.

scenes.visual: Joseph holds up his phone: a staff group message with a download link. Two answer cards bounce in: a check mark and a warning triangle.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A colleague posts in the staff group: “Free full version of the timetable program, no licence needed!” Safe or risky?

scenes.visual: The “risky” card gets the check badge. Four summary cards line up.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Risky: cracked software often carries malware, even when a colleague shares it. Remember: automatic updates, restart when asked, check the security date, and use only the official store.

scenes.visual: Joseph’s classroom. Pupils hold up green and red cards while he reads from a list; one pupil explains, pointing at the board.
scenes.animation: Cards pop up across the room.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: read out six short situations, like an update during an exam, or a cracked game from a friend. Pupils hold up green for safe and red for risky, and explain why.

checkpoints.prompt: An update is ready while you’re teaching all morning, and the battery is at 40%. What’s best?

options.text: Install it now, in the middle of the lesson
Let it install tonight on the charger and Wi-Fi

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: overnight on the charger and Wi-Fi is safe, free and out of your way.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: a restart mid-lesson is a problem, and “never” leaves the hole open. Let it run tonight on the charger.

checkpoints.prompt: A colleague posts in the staff group: “Free full version of the timetable program, no licence needed!” Safe or risky?

options.text: Risky: cracked software often hides malware

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: cracked copies are a favourite way to spread malware, whoever forwards them.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: your colleague means well, but cracked copies often hide malware. Use the official version.
